Proof of the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture (https://arxiv.org/html/2610.26686v1)
citeturn192view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"turn190view1","lineno":47}); Total lines: 420
L40: This question has been repeated many times over the years, with the oldest reference the authors could find dating back to 1970, both by Erdős with various coauthors [【22†22】, 【25†23】, 【23†25】, 【26†24】, 【27†26】, 【28†28】, 【29†29】, 【30†30】, 【24†21】], and by other authors [【31†18】, 【32†13】, 【33†14】, 【34†41】, 【16†2】, 【18†7】, 【35†44】, 【36†35】, 【37†34】, 【38†43】, 【39†32】, 【40†4】, 【41†1】, 【42†45】, 【43†31】, 【44†16】, 【45†52】, 【46†47】, 【47†42】, 【48†9】].
L41: Erdős and Szemerédi [【24†21】], proved that for any fixed $k\geq 3$ the answer is at most $2^{n-\Omega(\sqrt{n})}$ and conjectured that the answer should be exponentially smaller than $2^{n}$. Using improved uniform sunflower bounds of Kostochka [【49†40】], Deuber, Erdős, Gunderson, Kostochka, and Meyer [【31†18】] strengthened this to $2^{n-\sqrt{n\log\log n}/{\log\log\log n}}$ for large $n$.
L42: The breakthrough on the uniform problem due to Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, and Zhang [【40†4】], from 2019, improved the bound to $2^{n-n/(\log n)^{1+o(1)}}$. Subsequent refinements [【20†49】, 【50†6】] (in particular the one due to Rao [【20†49】]) give a slightly sharper bound of $2^{n-\Omega(n/\log n)}$, see [【40†4】, Theorem 4.1].
L43: For the special case of $k=3$, an important connection to additive combinatorics was established by Alon, Shpilka, and Umans [【16†2】], who showed that an exponential improvement over the trivial bound for cap sets in $\mathbb{F}_{3}^{n}$ would imply the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture in the $k=3$ case. Here, the polynomial-method breakthroughs of Croot, Lev, and Pach [【51†15】] and Ellenberg and Gijswijt [【52†19】] in 2016 supplied this cap-set estimate.
L44: Naslund and Sawin [【35†44】] then gave a direct argument giving the base of the exponent of ${3}/{2^{2/3}}\approx 1.89$ in the upper bound. Their proof, using Tao’s slice-rank formulation of the polynomial method [【53†53】], turns the absence of a sunflower into a diagonal tensor. The slice rank of that tensor measures the size of the family, while an expansion of its coordinatewise definition gives an upper bound.
L45: The same circle of ideas connects cap sets, tensors, and the group-theoretic approach to matrix multiplication [【18†7】].
L46: We prove the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture for every $k\geq 3$.
L47: ###### Theorem 1.
L48: 
L49: For every integer $k\geq 3$ and every integer $n\geq 1$, any subset of $2^{[n]}$ not containing a sunflower consisting of $k$ sets has size at most
L50: 
L51:  | $$3\left(2-\frac{1}{16k^{3}}\right)^{n}.$$  |
L52: We note that for $n<k-1$ the assumption is vacuous, so one may take the whole set $2^{[n]}$. For $n\geq k-1$, the above theorem, combined with the trivial bound of $2^{n}-1$ (coming from observing that singletons and the empty set always make a sunflower), shows that one can obtain a universal upper bound of $c_{k}^{n}$ for some $c_{k}<2$.
L53: The best known lower bound is due to Deuber, Erdős, Gunderson, Kostochka, and Meyer [【31†18】], who constructed $k$-sunflower-free families of size at least $\bigl(2-\frac{O(\log\log k)}{k}\bigr)^{n}$ for arbitrarily large $n$, showing that 【54†Theorem 1】 is not far from best possible for large $k$.
L54: ## 2 Proof ideas
L55: We prove Theorem 【54†1】 by first bounding sunflower-free families of vectors and then transferring this bound to set families. For $k=3$, Alon, Shpilka, and Umans [【16†2】, Section 2] showed that the Erdős–Szemerédi sunflower conjecture is equivalent to a power-saving bound in the alphabet size for the vector problem. Naslund and Sawin [【35†44】, Theorem 3] subsequently gave an explicit quantitative reduction from cap-set bounds, corresponding to the vector problem over a three-letter alphabet.
L56: We follow this approach for arbitrary $k$, with a modification of the reduction that improves the quantitative bound in the parameter range used here.
L57: To see how vectors arise, suppose that a ground set is split into $n$ disjoint blocks of size $D$. A set choosing exactly one element from each block can be recorded as a vector in $[D]^{n}$. Such sets form a sunflower precisely when, in every block, their chosen elements are either all equal or pairwise distinct. This gives the following formulation, which we will refer to as the vector sunflower problem of Alon, Shpilka, and Umans.
L58: ###### Definition.
L59: 
L60: For integers $k\geq 3$ and $D,n\geq 1$, a $k$-sunflower in $[D]^{n}$ is a collection of $k$ pairwise distinct vectors $\mathbf{x}_{0},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{k-1}\in[D]^{n}$ such that, in each coordinate, their entries are either all equal or pairwise distinct. Let $V_{k}(D,n)$ be the maximum size of a subset of $[D]^{n}$ containing no $k$-sunflower.
L61: For the reduction to the set problem, it suffices to find one fixed alphabet size $D$ and a constant $1\leq C<D$ such that $V_{k}(D,n)\leq C^{n}$ for every $n\geq 1$. In Section 【11†4】, we prove this implication for arbitrary $k$ using a probabilistic refinement of the block construction underlying the reduction of Naslund and Sawin. We average over random block choices within each family of sets of a fixed size, and then sum the resulting bounds over the possible sizes.
L62: This gives the quantitative saving needed for Theorem 【54†1】.
L63: For all integer $D\geq 3$, Naslund and Sawin [【35†44】, Theorem 2] proved
L64: 
L65:  | $$V_{3}(D,n)\leq\left(\frac{3(D-1)^{2/3}}{2^{2/3}}\right)^{n},$$  |
L66: 
L67: which establishes the power-saving upper bound for the case $k=3$ of the vector sunflower problem.
L68: Their proof uses a Fourier character expansion of a symmetric function that is nonzero precisely when its three entries are all equal or pairwise distinct. Each term in this expansion has a constant factor in at least one of the three variables. After multiplying across coordinates, some vector therefore contributes at most $2n/3$ nontrivial characters, and counting these character products gives the exponent $2/3$ of the alphabet size in their bound.
L69: Our main new ingredient is an interpolation construction of a local function for arbitrary $k$. We choose its nonzero values on all-distinct tuples to depend on the entries, and use successive interpolation to arrange that every term has a polynomial factor of degree at most $k-2$ in one of the last $k-1$ variables, with the remaining factor independent of that variable. These low-degree factors all lie in a common space of dimension $k-1$.

L225: Substitute this representation into the coordinatewise product defining $T_{c}$ and expand. Every resulting monomial has the form
L226: 
L227:  | $$M=\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\prod_{r=1}^{n}(\mathbf{x}_{i})_{r}^{d_{i,r}},$$  |
L228: where $0\leq d_{i,r}\leq D-1$. For each coordinate $r\in[n]$, there is some $i\in[k-1]$ such that $d_{i,r}\leq k-2$. By the pigeonhole principle, some $i\in[k-1]$ satisfies this inequality for at least $n/(k-1)$ coordinates. Consequently, the number of coordinates with $d_{i,r}\geq k-1$ is at most $n-n/(k-1)=(1-1/(k-1))n.$
L229: 
L230: Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space of functions on $[D]^{n}$ spanned by the monomial functions
L231:  | $$\mathbf{x}\longmapsto\prod_{r=1}^{n}x_{r}^{d_{r}},\qquad\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}),$$  |
L232: 
L233: whose integer exponents satisfy $0\leq d_{r}\leq D-1$ for every $r\in[n]$, and
L234: 
L235:  | $$\bigl|\{r\in[n]:d_{r}\geq k-1\}\bigr|\leq(1-1/(k-1))n.$$  |
L236: 
L237: For each monomial $M$, choose an index $i\in[k-1]$ supplied by the pigeonhole argument and write
L238:  | $$M=\left(\prod_{r=1}^{n}(\mathbf{x}_{i})_{r}^{d_{i,r}}\right)\left(\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq\ell\leq k-1\\
L239: \ell\neq i\end{subarray}}\prod_{r=1}^{n}(\mathbf{x}_{\ell})_{r}^{d_{\ell,r}}\right).$$  |
L240: The first factor is an element of $\mathcal{P}$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_{i}$, while the second factor is independent of $\mathbf{x}_{i}$. Grouping these terms and expressing their first factors in a basis of $\mathcal{P}$ therefore gives the decomposition required in Lemma 【56†3】. Since $T_{c}$ is a sunflower tester by Observation 【60†5】, Lemma 【57†4】 yields $V_{k}(D,n)\leq\dim\mathcal{P}$.
L241: Finally, we count the monomials spanning $\mathcal{P}$ according to the number $s$ of coordinates whose exponents are at least $k-1$. There are $\binom{n}{s}$ choices for these coordinates, $D-k+1$ choices for each of their exponents, and $k-1$ choices for each remaining exponent. Therefore,
L242: 
L243:  | $$V_{k}(D,n)\leq\dim\mathcal{P}\leq\sum_{s=0}^{(1-1/(k-1))n}\binom{n}{s}(D-k+1)^{s}(k-1)^{n-s}.$$  |
L244: 
L245: This completes the proof. ∎
L246: Combined with a simple application of Chernoff’s inequality, Lemma 【61†7】 yields the proof of Theorem 【55†2】.
L247: ###### Proof of Theorem 【55†2】.
L248: 
L249: If $D\leq 4k^{2}$, the desired bound follows from the trivial bound $V_{k}(D,n)\leq D^{n}$, so we may assume $D>4k^{2}$. We estimate the sum in Lemma 【61†7】 by a multiplicative Chernoff bound [【62†3】, Theorem A.1.12] telling us that $\mathbb{P}(\textrm{Bin}(n,(k-1)/D)\geq n/(k-1))\leq(4k^{2}/D)^{n/(k-1)}$. In particular,
L250:  | $\displaystyle V_{k}(D,n)$  | $\displaystyle\leq D^{n}\sum_{s=0}^{(1-1/(k-1))n}\binom{n}{s}\left(1-\frac{k-1}{D}\right)^{s}\left(\frac{k-1}{D}\right)^{n-s}\leq\bigl((4k^{2})^{1/(k-1)}\cdot D^{1-1/(k-1)}\bigr)^{n},$  |
L251: 
L252: as desired. ∎
L253: ## 4 Reduction from vectors to sets
L254: 
L255: We now transfer the vector sunflower bound to the set family setting. A probabilistic refinement of the argument of Naslund and Sawin [【35†44】] yields the following quantitative version.
L256: ###### Proposition 8.
L257: 
L258: Let $D\geq 2$ be an integer, and suppose that for some constant $C$ with $1\leq C<D$, we have $V_{k}(D,n)\leq C^{n},$ for every $n\geq 1$. Let $\rho=C/D$. Then, for every integer $N\geq 1$, any subset of $2^{[N]}$ not containing a $k$-sunflower has size at most
L259: 
L260:  | $$(1+\rho^{-1})(1+\rho^{1/(D-1)})^{N}.$$  |
L261: ###### Proof.
L262: Take $\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{[N]}$ with no $k$-sunflower. For $0\leq s\leq N$, let $\mathcal{F}_{s}$ be the sets in $\mathcal{F}$ of size $s$, i.e. $\mathcal{F}_{s}=\{F\in\mathcal{F}:|F|=s\}$. Now fix $s$, and let $t:=\min\{s,\lfloor\frac{N-s}{D-1}\rfloor\}$. Take a permutation of $[N]$ uniformly at random. Let its first $Dt$ elements form ordered sets $B_{1},\ldots,B_{t}$, each of size $D$, and its next $s-t$ elements form a set $R$.
L263: The existence of such $B_{1},\ldots,B_{t},R$ is guaranteed by our choice of $t$. If $t>0$, then we define $\mathcal{G}$ by the family of sets obtained by taking the union of $R$ with exactly one element from each $B_{i}$, i.e., $\mathcal{G}=\{R\cup\{b_{1},b_{2},\ldots,b_{t}\}:b_{i}\in B_{i}\}$. If $t=0$, set $\mathcal{G}=\{R\}$. In either case, $|\mathcal{G}|=D^{t}$.
L264: Then we can view each element in $\mathcal{G}$ as a vector in $[D]^{t}$ by identifyng each element $v=R\cup\{b_{1,j_{1}},\dots,b_{t,j_{t}}\}\in\mathcal{G}$ with the tuple $(j_{1},\dots,j_{t})\in[D]^{t}$, where $b_{i,j_{i}}$ is the $j_{i}$-th element of $B_{i}$ in the prescribed order for each $i\in[t]$.
L265: Since $\mathcal{F}_{s}$ contains no $k$-sunflower, the set of vectors in $[D]^{t}$ corresponding to $\mathcal{F}_{s}\cap\mathcal{G}$ contains no $k$-sunflower either. Indeed, if $k$ such vectors formed a $k$-sunflower, then in each block $B_{i}$, their chosen elements would be either all the same or pairwise distinct. In the former case, that common element would belong to the core, while in the latter case, $B_{i}$ would contribute nothing to any pairwise intersection.
L266: Since every set also contains the common fixed part $R$, the corresponding $k$ sets would therefore form a $k$-sunflower in $\mathcal{F}_{s}$, a contradiction. Hence, $|\mathcal{F}_{s}\cap\mathcal{G}|\leq V_{k}(D,t)\leq C^{t}$.
L267: By symmetry, every $s$-element subset of $[N]$ has the same probability of belonging to $\mathcal{G}$. Indeed, for any two $s$-element subsets $S_{1},S_{2}\subseteq[N]$, there exists a permutation of $[N]$ sending $S_{1}$ to $S_{2}$. Since $\mathcal{G}$ is generated from a uniformly random permutation of $[N]$, relabeling the ground set by any fixed permutation leaves the distribution of $\mathcal{G}$ unchanged. This gives $\mathbb{P}(S_{1}\in\mathcal{G})=\mathbb{P}(S_{2}\in\mathcal{G})$.
L268: Hence, for every $s$-element subset $S\subseteq[N]$, we have $\mathbb{P}(S\in\mathcal{G})=|\mathcal{G}|/\binom{N}{s}=D^{t}/\binom{N}{s}$.

L16: > Abstract:Let $f(k,s)$ denote the minimum integer $m$ such that any family $\mathcal{F}$ consisting of $k$-sized sets of cardinality at least $m$ always contain a sunflower of size $s$. The Erdős-Rado Sunflower Conjecture states that for every $s >2$, there is an constant $C=C(s)$ such that $f(k,s) \leq C^k$. In this paper, we prove the conjecture for shifted families.
